analysis.one_liner: Bans most application, screening, and late fees for renters and requires landlords to disclose the true monthly cost before a lease is signed.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its referral to two House committees in July 2023, no action was taken before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned landlords of federally backed rental housing from charging renters application fees and tenant screening fees, and would have banned late fees unless the money is credited back toward rent. It would have stopped landlords from using credit scores and nationwide consumer reports to screen applicants, and would have required them to tell renters — before a lease is signed — the full monthly cost including fees, any litigation history with tenants, ongoing pest or maintenance problems, and the rent increases at the property over the past 10 years. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would have had 180 days to define "junk fee" for rentals and make it an unfair debt-collection practice to report unpaid junk fees to credit bureaus. The bill covered any unit receiving federal housing assistance or on a property with a federally backed mortgage — which reaches most rentals, since most apartment building loans go through Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, or USDA.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters — especially first-time applicants and households with thin or damaged credit — in any rental unit on a property with a federally backed mortgage or receiving federal housing assistance. They would save application and screening fees every time they move, could no longer be hit with late fees that never come back, and would learn the full monthly cost and the property's rent-increase history before signing a lease. Tenants would also be protected from junk fees being reported to credit bureaus.

how_it_helps.text: It bans application fees and tenant screening fees, so a household could apply to rent a covered unit without paying for the landlord's background check.
It bans late fees unless the amount is credited back against the next month's rent, so late fees could no longer be pure profit.
It bars landlords from using credit scores or nationwide consumer reports when screening applicants, which removes a barrier for renters with thin or damaged credit.

Before a lease is signed, the landlord would have to disclose the total monthly amount due including fees, any history of litigation with tenants, ongoing pest and maintenance problems, and the rent increases at the property over the previous 10 years.

It directs the CFPB to define 'junk fee' for rental housing within 180 days and to treat reporting an unpaid junk fee to credit bureaus as an unlawful debt-collection practice, keeping junk fees from damaging renters' credit.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property managers of federally backed rental properties, who would lose fee income (application fees, screening fees, late-fee revenue) and would have to disclose litigation history, maintenance problems, and 10 years of rent increases before leasing. Tenant screening companies and credit reporting agencies would lose business from the ban on charging applicants for background checks and on using nationwide consumer reports in screening.

drawbacks.text: Banning application and screening fees does not make the underlying costs disappear, so landlords subject to the ban could reasonably fold those costs into rent or adopt stricter self-screening criteria, meaning some savings could be passed back as higher rents or fewer offers to applicants with weaker histories.

Prohibiting the use of credit scores and nationwide consumer reports in tenant screening removes a standard risk tool landlords use, which could raise landlords' perceived risk and make some of them less willing to rent to unfamiliar applicants.

The required disclosures — a summary of past litigation with tenants, ongoing pest and maintenance issues, and 10 years of rent increases — could be burdensome for small landlords to compile and is not defined in detail.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for renters in the huge swath of housing touched by federal mortgage programs: hundreds of dollars saved per move, no more late fees compounding debt, and more upfront information before signing a lease. The drawbacks are real but manageable: landlords argue the fee bans do not remove their underlying costs, so rent or stricter applicant standards may absorb them; the credit-report ban could make screening harder for small landlords and potentially help applicants with serious recent housing history; and the 10-year rent history disclosure could burden small owners. On balance the bill was a straightforward consumer-protection measure whose main losers would be fee-dependent landlords and the tenant-screening industry, not renters. Its fatal weakness was political: it had no Republican support and died in committee without a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Financial Services and Veterans' Affairs committees in July 2023, one of them passed it down to a subcommittee a month later, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 26, 2023, and referred the same day to the House Financial Services Committee and the House Veterans' Affairs Committee.
On August 24, 2023, the Veterans' Affairs Committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity — the last recorded action.
No hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded on the bill in either committee for the remainder of the 118th Congress.
Congress.gov records no further action after the subcommittee referral; the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords, property managers, and tenant-screening companies keep collecting application, screening, and late fees without the new disclosure requirements, and the committees' leadership never had to take a position.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the two Republican committee chairs who controlled whether the bill got a hearing never scheduled one; no Republican is recorded as supporting it.

industries.industry: Landlords and property managers (especially large operators of federally backed rental properties)
industries.note: They would lose application fees, screening fees, and profitable late fees on the vast universe of rentals with a federal mortgage behind the property, and would face new pre-lease disclosure duties. The bill's remedies all fall on them, so their interest ran against the bill while renters' interest ran for it.

The bill bans charging tenants for criminal-history and consumer-report background checks and also bars landlords from using nationwide consumer reports for screening, shrinking the market these companies sell to.

They would lose landlords' use of nationwide consumer reports for tenant screening, but the bill's CFPB rule would stop landlords from reporting unpaid junk fees to the bureaus — a change that protects consumers' credit files at some cost to fee-collection leverage.
